newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH FIXED BOND YIELDS SEEN FLAT AT TENDER.
newsitem.headline: POLISH FIXED BOND YIELDS SEEN FLAT AT TENDER.

text.p: The average yields of Poland's 16-percent two-year bond and 12-percent five-year bond are expected to hold flat at Thursday's joint 800 million zloty primary auction, analysts said on Wednesday.
At the last auction of similar two- and five-year fixed bonds on September 19, the averge yield for the shorter paper was 19.95 and 18.10 percent for the longer bond.
"The treasury is not likely to raise yields at Thursday's auction after keeping them flat for several previous tenders," said Marcin Rzechowski of PBI SA.
Analysts expected Thursday's tender to be undersubscribed with demand for both terms totalling some 600 million zlotys.
They said foreign investors should bid only for small amounts at the tender after uninspiring September inflation data faded prospects of slower price growth this year.
At the last auction the treasury sold 253 million zlotys of two-year bonds at an average price of 93.62 and 42 million five-year bonds at an average price of 80.95.
Thursday's auction is the treasury's first of four offers of a new series of two- and five-year fixed bonds, which mature on February 12, 1999 and February 12, 2002 respectively.
The value date for this tender is November 5, 1996, for the two-year bonds and November 12, 1996, for the five-year paper.
Analysts said demand should focus on the two-year bonds, which were an attractive longer-term Polish instrument for large institutional investors, not concerned about liquidity.

"The two-year bond is actually the best product available on the market for those who have to invest money in longer term instruments and are not very concerned about liquidity, such as insurance companies," an analyst at investment company said.
Analysts said the two-year paper was a bargain compared to the 52-week T-bills, whose maximium yield was 19.46 percent at last Monday's primary tender.
Some said however that some domestic banks were already heavily exposed to bonds and may bid for higher yields.
"Some banks seem to have swamped bond positions, which may leave them space for testing better-than-secondary market prices," said Marcin Rzechowski from PBI SA.
In secondary trade the two-year bond bid around 20 percent.
Analysts said yields should be supported by September's higher-than-expected 1.9 percent rise in consumer prices, which took the year-on-year index to 19.5 percent from August's 20.5.
They said the 1.9 percent price rise, against expectations of 1.4 percent, pushed the government's 1996 inflation target of year-on-year 17 percent out of reach.
